newsitem.title: INDIA: Rao's plight gives Indian premier breathing space.
newsitem.headline: Rao's plight gives Indian premier breathing space.

text.p: The resignation of former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao from the leadership of the Congress party gives a new lease of life to the nation's centre-left coalition government, analysts said on Sunday.

Rao's abrupt decision to quit the Congress presidency on Saturday after a court ruling in a criminal cheating case hastened the decline of India's oldest party and offered Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda political breathing room, they said.
"Deve Gowda is enormously strengthened by disarray in Congress," Vinod Mehta, editor of Outlook magazine, told Reuters.
"It now is more remote that Congress will try to precipitate a crisis which would lead to general elections," said Pran Chopra of the Centre for Policy Research, an independent think-tank.

Rao stepped down after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear as a co-accused in a $100,000 cheating case. An Indian expatriate businessman alleges Rao and a Hindu guru conspired to cheat him of the money in 1983.
The former prime minister, who launched India on the road to a more open economy in 1991 but was handed defeat in general elections ended last May, says he is innocent.
Despite his party's humiliating second place finish at the polls, Rao has continued to play a pivotal role in national politics.

Deve Gowda's 13-party coalition, ranging from free-trade centrists to communists, lacks an outright majority in parliament. Rao's Congress has held the key to the government's survival with its 140 seats in the 545-member house.

Despite Rao's legal woes -- he is also under investigation in a vote-buying case -- such is his legendary political acumen that there has been periodic speculation ever since Deve Gowda took office in June that Congress might provoke a crisis.
Now, with Rao on the sidelines and Congress set for a struggle to find a successor, Deve Gowda can heave a sigh of relief, analysts said.

"This gives a great boost to Deve Gowda," said Chandan Mitra, editor of The Pioneer newspaper. "I would not be surprised if Deve Gowda started fishing in troubled waters, instigating rivalries in Congress."

A significant segment of Congress's 140 deputies are keen to move beyond offering simple outside support to Deve Gowda and join the government, which has pursued the same liberal economic path which Rao first blazed.
"The chance of Congress participating in the Deve Gowda government is definitely brighter," Mitra said.

Rao's resignation came at a crucial juncture for Congress, which has been hoping for a revival of its fortunes in assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state with 140 million people. The polls start on September 30.
Now Congress, which was set to select a provisional leader on Monday, may end up struggling in the big northern state.
"The party is facing the most difficult crisis in its 111-year history," Mitra said.

Chopra said Rao's departure was part of a long-term decline in the influence of Congress, which was the nation's political touchstone before and after independence but has since lost much relevancy for a more divided, caste-conscious electorate.
"Congress began to sink under the weight of corruption charges. It is gradually losing its undefined and comprehensive character," Chopra told Reuters.
"It signifies the final nail in the coffin of a single party of hegemony. It deepens the phenomenon of coalition politics."
While a string of cases aimed at political leaders may reflect worrisome and deep-seated corruption, the courts' determination to chase even the most powerful was heartening, analysts said.
"Foreign investors have to be reassured that the legal process in this country does work," Mehta said. "They may be frustrated by the speed, but it works, even against the powerful and rich."
